extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students in probability theory / mathematical statistics
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, hypotheses, and proof-conditions for central limit, local limit, Berry–Esseen, and Poisson limit theorems and related lemmas; includes classification of lattice vs nonlattice distributions and Poisson process characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Kac central limit theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: For g(n) = number of distinct prime divisors of n, as n → ∞, Pn({m ≤ n : (g(m) − log log n)/√(log log n) ≤ x}) → Φ(x) (standard normal c.d.f.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate g(n) by sum of independent indicators δp(n) for primes p ≤ n with P(δp = 1) = 1/p. Show one can ignore primes near n (choose αn = n^{1/log log n}) so that the truncated sum Sn has mean and variance ≈ log log n and apply the CLT (Theorem 3.4.10) to the independent model Xp. Control moments and show moments of empirical sum converge to moments of normal via the moment method (use bounds for contributions of large primes and for higher moments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Berry–Esseen bound (Theorem 3.4.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1, X2, ... are i.i.d. with EXi = 0, var(Xi) = σ^2 > 0 and ρ = E|Xi|^3 < ∞, and Fn(x) is distribution of (X1 + ... + Xn)/(σ√n), then sup_x |Fn(x) − Φ(x)| ≤ 3ρ/(σ^3√n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inequality holds for all n and x; the ρ < ∞ (third absolute moment) hypothesis is necessary to obtain the n^{−1/2} rate. Constants can be improved (historic improvements cited). Proof uses characteristic functions, smoothing (Polya density), and comparison of ch.f.'s; remarks explain that the bound is nontrivial for n ≥ ~10 and that E|X|^{2+δ} criteria give refined summability results (Heyde).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of third moment for n^{-1/2} rate (remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis E|X|^3 < ∞ is needed to get the rate n^{−1/2}; more generally, for 0 < δ < 1, ∑ n^{-1+δ/2} sup_x |Fn(x) − Φ(x)| < ∞ iff E|X|^{2+δ} < ∞ (Heyde 1967).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a sharpness/necessity remark accompanying Berry–Esseen; used to judge when rates of convergence results apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trichotomy for characteristic functions / classification (Theorem 3.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For ϕ(t) = E e^{itX}, exactly one of: (i) |ϕ(t)| < 1 for all t ≠ 0 (nonlattice), (ii) there is λ > 0 with |ϕ(λ)| = 1 and |ϕ(t)| < 1 for 0 < t < λ (lattice with span 2π/λ), (iii) |ϕ(t)| = 1 for all t (degenerate; X constant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence between |ϕ(t)| = 1 at some t and X being concentrated on a lattice b + (2π/t)Z is used. This classification is the basis for deciding whether to use lattice vs nonlattice local limit theorems and for checking periodicity/arithmetic cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: lattice distribution and span / arithmetic case
rubrics_metrics.description: X has a lattice distribution if ∃ b, h > 0 with P(X ∈ b + hZ) = 1. The largest such h is the span. If b = 0 (P(X ∈ hZ) = 1) the distribution is arithmetic (then ϕ is periodic with period 2π/h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine applicability of lattice local limit theorem (Theorem 3.5.3). Example: symmetric ±1 has span 2 (choose b = −1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local limit theorem — lattice case (Theorem 3.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xi i.i.d., EXi = 0, var(Xi) = σ^2 ∈ (0, ∞), common lattice distribution with span h, Sn = sum Xi. Define pn(x) = P(Sn/√n = x) for x in lattice Ln = {(nb + hz)/√n}. Then n^{1/2} h · sup_{x∈Ln} |pn(x) − n(x)| → 0, where n(x) = (2πσ^2)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/(2σ^2)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses characteristic function inversion adapted to the discrete lattice (finite integral over a compact interval determined by h), division of integral into small/large t regions, bounds on |ϕ(t)| and dominated convergence. Practical rule: approximate point probabilities on lattice by Gaussian density times h/√n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local limit theorem — nonlattice case (Theorem 3.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xi i.i.d., EXi = 0, var(Xi) = σ^2 ∈ (0, ∞), and common characteristic function ϕ(t) satisfies |ϕ(t)| < 1 for all t ≠ 0, then for x_n/√n → x and any a < b, √n·P(Sn ∈ (x_n + a, x_n + b)) → (b − a) n(x) (Gaussian density at x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof requires 'smoothing' via convolution with a Polya density hθ to control bad characteristic functions and then inversion + dominated convergence. Use when distribution is nonlattice; gives convergence of scaled interval probabilities to Gaussian mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson convergence — basic limit theorem (Theorem 3.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_{n,m}, 1 ≤ m ≤ n be independent Bernoulli with P(X_{n,m}=1)=p_{n,m}. If (i) ∑_{m=1}^n p_{n,m} → λ ∈ (0,∞) and (ii) max_{m} p_{n,m} → 0, then S_n = ∑ X_{n,m} ⇒ Poisson(λ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs given: characteristic function approach (product-of-moment-generating-terms) and a total-variation approach using convolution/metric lemmas. Intuition: many rare independent events with small probabilities and total mean λ produce Poisson limit (law of rare events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Total variation distance criteria and basic lemmas (Lemmas 3.6.4–3.6.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and useful inequalities for total variation distance kµ − νk on ℤ: (i) kµ_n − µk → 0 iff µ_n(x) → µ(x) ∀x (equivalent to weak convergence for countable support); (ii) product measure bound: kµ1×µ2 − ν1×ν2k ≤ kµ1 − ν1k + kµ2 − ν2k; (iii) convolution bound: kµ1∗µ2 − ν1∗ν2k ≤ kµ1×µ2 − ν1×ν2k; (iv) single-Bernoulli vs Poisson bound: if µ has µ(1)=p, µ(0)=1−p and ν is Poisson(p) then kµ − νk ≤ p^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inequalities let one bound total-variation distance between sums and their Poisson approximations by summing p_{n,m}^2 terms (Hodges–Le Cam approach), leading to explicit error bounds (see eq. (3.6.1)). Useful for quantifying approximation quality and proving convergence in stronger metrics than weak convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodges–Le Cam Poisson approximation bound (eq. (3.6.1))
rubrics_metrics.description: If µn is distribution of S_n = ∑ X_{n,m} and νn is Poisson with mean λ_n = ∑ p_{n,m}, then kµn − νnk ≤ 2 ∑_{m=1}^n p_{n,m}^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of the product/convolution/one-Bernoulli bounds above. Under p_{n,m}=1/n this yields total variation error O(1/n). Stein's method gives sharper bounds of order (λ ∨ 1)^{-1} ∑ p_{n,m}^2 in some settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson approximation heuristics / rate examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When p_{n,m} = 1/n, the total-variation bound is O(1/n); comparison with exact binomial-to-Poisson probabilities shows the largest discrepancy typically occurs at k=1 and is about (3/4)e/n in the example, while some cases (matching problem) have much faster convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inclusion–exclusion and exact expansions to gauge actual error in concrete combinatorial examples (matching, occupancy) where dependence exists; sometimes obtain much better rates than generic bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson convergence for nonnegative integer-valued variables (Theorem 3.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_{n,m} be independent nonnegative integer-valued with P(X_{n,m}=1)=p_{n,m}, P(X_{n,m}≥2)=r_{n,m}. If (i) ∑ p_{n,m} → λ ∈ (0,∞), (ii) max p_{n,m} → 0, (iii) ∑ r_{n,m} → 0, then S_n = ∑ X_{n,m} ⇒ Poisson(λ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to Bernoulli case by replacing each X_{n,m} with indicator of being 1 and showing that contributions ≥2 are negligible (converging together lemma). Use when components are rare single events but multiple-event probabilities vanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson process characterization (Theorem 3.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A counting process N(·) on [0,∞) is Poisson with rate λ (i.e., N(0,t) ~ Poisson(λt)) if it satisfies: (i) independent increments over disjoint intervals; (ii) stationary increments (distribution of N(s,t) depends only on t−s); (iii) P(N(0,h)=1)=λh + o(h); (iv) P(N(0,h)≥2)=o(h) as h→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction/intuition: partition interval and apply Theorem 3.7.1; equivalently construct Poisson process via i.i.d. exponential(λ) interarrival times T_n differences (renewal construction) and use memoryless property of exponential to verify independent increments and stationarity. Conditions (iii)–(iv) express 'rare events' and rule out multiple simultaneous arrivals in vanishing intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exponential memoryless property and consequences (3.7.1 remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: If T ~ Exponential(λ) then P(T > t + s | T > t) = P(T > s); this lack-of-memory implies that the location of first arrival after time t is independent of the past and exponential, which underpins renewal construction of Poisson processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to show that arrivals after a time t are independent of the count up to t and have the same law as the original process; yields independent increments and the explicit Poisson probabilities for N(t).
